Senses.Explanation: Within the Caodong Five Ranks, the relative within the absolute (正中偏) names differentiated appearance within the absolute or upright. Records identify it relationally and then test it through verses, images, and contrast with the absolute within the relative (偏中正). Caoshan Benji explains that the upright position is the empty realm and the partial position the realm of forms; he glosses the relative within the absolute (正中偏) as turning from principle toward affairs and elsewhere as the lord looking toward the minister. Hongzhi Zhengjue's Five Ranks verse gives the rank a night image in which a wooden boy strikes the moon's door and wakes a jade woman. The Mirror of Humans and Devas records an unnamed monastic asking Fenyang Shanzhao for this rank and preserves Fenyang's moon-and-cock response. Langting Ting gives it swallows murmuring between roof beams. Juelang Daosheng relates it to an eastern circle and lesser yang, while Ruibai Mingxue identifies his own shout as this rank once he has mounted the seat. Tianran Hanshi transmits an older night-and-moon verse whose historical author is not established in the available six-rung evidence and then offers his own matching verse, showing that no single image exhausts the relation.
